headline: Chip-led bounce holds, but Gulf tensions keep the tape cautious
body: Monday's relief rally largely held: the Nasdaq Composite closed up about 1.1% and the S&P 500 added roughly 0.4%, with the Dow essentially flat, as semiconductor names that led last week's rout did the leading again. SanDisk jumped around 7% and other chip names extended their bounce, reinforcing the sense that last week's AI-infrastructure jitters were more of a sharp, narrow unwind than a broad repricing. That composure faded a little heading into Tuesday's open, though. Premarket futures turned mixed and cautious, with the Dow modestly higher but S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures both slipping, after Iran raised the specter of targeting undersea communications cables near the Strait of Hormuz, reviving the geopolitical risk premium that's kept Brent crude hovering close to $100 a barrel and gasoline near $4 a gallon in recent weeks.

The inflation conversation is getting tangled up in that same energy story. Treasury Secretary Bessent has been framing the recent pickup in headline CPI (running near 3.5% versus a cooler ~2.3% core) as an energy-shock problem tied to the Gulf conflict rather than a demand or tariff issue, a distinction that matters for how traders read the Fed's next moves and why 10-year yields have stayed elevated even as growth data stays decent. Retail and social-media chatter was thin and non-specific in today's search results, so this read leans more on price action, sector leadership, and the macro/geopolitical headline flow than on any clear crowd signal. Netflix's earnings after today's close add a near-term, stock-specific catalyst that could either reinforce the tentative tech stabilization or reopen the skepticism that hit growth names last week.
